summary.en-US: Vim keys for Firefox that teach themselves: link hints, a command line, keyboard drag and drop, and a popup that shows what every key does.

description.en-US:
Desert the mouse. The keys teach themselves.

DesertFox puts Vim keys in Firefox. Press f and a short label appears next to every link and button. Type the label to click it. Press j and k to scroll, / to search the page, and : to run any command by name, with completion.

If you know Vim, you already know DesertFox. Modes, hjkl, gg and G, yy, counts, registers, marks, macros and . all work as you expect. Two keys differ: v puts a caret in the page and V starts a selection. If you do not know Vim, you need five keys on the first day: j, k, f, : and g? for help.

You do not memorize the keys
- A which-key popup lists the keys that can follow and what each does. It opens after a short pause on a key that starts a longer sequence, such as g. Alt+? opens it in normal, hint, caret and visual mode.
- A Quick Start page opens after you install DesertFox. It teaches the first keys, and it shows your own keys if you rebind them.
- A Practice page has 15 short lessons, from scrolling to video. You do each task on the page, and the page ticks it off.
- The help page lists every key and command. DesertFox generates it from your keymap, so it is always current.

You drag and drop from the keyboard
- Grab and move: press ;Gg and type the label on a slider or a card. Then h, j, k and l move it, [ and ] halve and double the step, Enter drops it and Escape cancels.
- Grab and drop: press ;gg, type the label on the element, then type the label on the place it goes to.
- Press ;w to swipe a carousel with the same keys.
- Keyboard drag is built in. It needs no script and no helper program. It works with sliders, sortable lists and drag-and-drop boards. A drag stays inside one frame, and a page that accepts only real mouse input ignores it.

It tells you what went wrong
A typo in a key, a command or a config line is an error with a message, never a silent no-op.

More
- Link hints with filters and actions: click, double-click, hover, focus, inspect in DevTools, open in a background tab, copy a link, download a file, and more.
- A command line with completion over tabs, history, bookmarks, commands and settings.
- Caret and visual mode to select and copy text with Vim motions.
- Macros, registers, marks, quickmarks and your own search engines.
- Keys for tabs, windows, containers, tab sessions, and video and audio.
- Video and audio keys: seek, speed, volume, captions, frame step, picture-in-picture and quality.
- Rules per site, and built-in keys for Google Sheets, Maps and Drive and for search and news result lists. Alt+l starts an arrow mode that presses the arrow keys on the focused control.
- A settings page, 29 built-in themes, and a config that you export and import as a zip.
- A new tab page with a clock and your links, and optional weather and IP cards.

Safe by design
DesertFox never runs the keys, commands or config lines you type as code. The only exception is a snippet (a JavaScript file for your own command). You write it in your own config or import it with your consent, and it runs in the page you name.

Optional native host (Linux only)
You do not need it. Firefox does not let extensions read files or start programs. A small helper program adds three things: editing a text field in your own editor, keys that open Firefox pages, and config files in ~/.config/desertfox/. You install it yourself with a command that DesertFox shows and you paste into a terminal. Then you grant the nativeMessaging permission with a button. The helper takes a fixed set of requests and has no shell. Its source is in the repository.

Optional browser module (Linux only, off by default)
You do not need it. Without it, the tab and scroll keys stop on pages that an extension cannot reach, and on a page that is still loading. The module is a small script that is not part of this add-on. You install it yourself, with administrator rights, into the folder where Firefox loads its own startup scripts. It then handles the keys that move between tabs and scroll the page on those pages, before the page sees them. DesertFox never installs it or loads it. You turn on the setting browser_module to let DesertFox share the on or off switch, the keys that move tabs and scroll, each tab's mode and the blur_on_load setting with it. It also takes the other DesertFox keys that need no page, such as closing a tab or going back, and sends DesertFox only the finished match, the keys and the count, never raw key presses. The module sends DesertFox its version number. DesertFox sends it a fixed list of commands with checked arguments and never code. When you press a pane key, DesertFox also asks it to change the window: split the window, unsplit, close both tabs of a split, resize a split or move the focus to the sidebar, page, other pane or DevTools. It answers with a short refusal text. DesertFox also sends it a short table of keys for DevTools, each with one of four tree moves, so j, k, h and l move through the DevTools trees. With the module, gB labels the controls of Firefox itself (toolbars, tabs, menus, permission prompts, the downloads panel, dialogs, the Library and Page Info) as link hints label a page, and j, k, h and l walk open menus and panels. A hint that would grant something, such as Allow on a permission prompt or opening a download, only marks the control. It waits for an Enter that you type, and no message can confirm it. Hints send DesertFox the control numbers, boxes in pixels and the keys you type while labels show, and nothing leaves your device. Its source is in the repository.
A second setting, browser_module_pages, also off by default, lets the module run DesertFox's own page code inside the PDF viewer and Reader View, so hints and caret mode work there. With it on, DesertFox puts a copy of your keys and site rules, your settings and your theme where the module can read them, and the messages between that page code and DesertFox pass through the module. They can hold text from those pages, such as link text and text you copy. All of it stays on your device.

Privacy
DesertFox has no account, no telemetry and no analytics. Settings and state stay in Firefox storage on your device. Two optional new tab cards contact a server: the weather card (Open-Meteo, after you allow location information from its button) and the IP info line (Cloudflare, off by default). The privacy policy lists exactly what each sends.

DesertFox runs in Firefox on desktop. An extension cannot run on the pages of Firefox itself, such as about: pages, the PDF viewer and Reader View. The optional browser module above is the one way to take the tab and scroll keys there.

Source code, issues and docs: https://github.com/uhs-robert/desertfox

version.approval_notes:
Build: BUILD.md at the root of the source archive lists the steps: Node 26, npm ci, node tools/release_stamp.mjs <version>, npm run build. The output is dist/. The xpi is dist/ without the *.map files. The stamp step writes dist/host_sha256.json, the SHA-256 of this release's native host scripts.

Remote code: the add-on loads no remote code and does not use the userScripts API. Every script and page is in the package. Requests the add-on makes by itself go to fixed hosts: api.open-meteo.com, geocoding-api.open-meteo.com and air-quality-api.open-meteo.com (optional weather card, after the user grants the optional locationInfo data collection from a button) and 1.1.1.1/cdn-cgi/trace (optional IP info line, off by default). Both send no cookies and no referrer. Two things load from addresses the user's pages give: the command line shows each open tab's icon from the http or https address the page gave, and the copy and save image commands fetch the image from its page.

Snippets: tabs.executeScript with a code string runs only a snippet that the user wrote in their own config folder or imported. Every import shows each snippet's code and asks for consent per snippet before storing it. The add-on ships no snippet and fetches none from a developer server. Content script keys never evaluate strings.

Native host: nativeMessaging is an optional permission, requested from a button on the :native.install page. The host is a Linux-only Python script with a fixed set of verbs and no shell or eval verb (host/README.md). Its install command and its optional self update (off by default, setting host_auto_update) download scripts from this repository's GitHub releases over HTTPS. Both check each script against SHA-256 hashes that ship inside this signed add-on (host_sha256.json) and refuse a script that does not match. The host is not in the add-on package.

Browser module: a separate, optional script, not in the add-on package and not installed or loaded by the add-on. Its source folder is browser_module/ in the repository. The user installs it with sudo into Firefox's own startup folder, and it runs with browser privileges outside the extension. The add-on contains no code that installs, downloads or runs it. The setting browser_module is off by default and a consent setting: an imported config cannot turn it on. While it is on, the add-on writes to its own storage.session a table of at most 32 single-key bindings (a key and a command id from a fixed list of seven tab, scroll and stop-loading commands, with checked arguments), the on or off switch, each tab's mode with a flag that says its content script is live, and whether its blur_on_load setting is on. When the module draws its status bar, the add-on adds per tab the half-typed keys (at most 8), a typed count, a pass-next flag, a recording register and, outside private windows, a site mode label, plus the mode colors of the theme and the bar's item lists and corner style from the settings. The add-on reads back a hello (a protocol version number, a version string and a flag that says the status bar is drawn, capped at 256 bytes) and a short list of typed messages (at most 16, and 4 KB or a kind's own limit of at most 64 KB). Each message names a kind from a fixed allow list, with checked arguments. A message of any other kind, or over its kind's limit, is refused. The add-on reads the hello at most once a second and the list at most every 50 ms, and checks them field by field. In the other direction, the add-on writes typed pane requests from a fixed list of six kinds (split with a new tab, split with the next tab, unsplit, close both, resize by whole 5 percent steps, focus the sidebar, page, other pane or DevTools). They change the browser window only when the user runs a pane command, by its key or from the DesertFox command line. The module checks that list the same way, field by field. The module answers each with a short refusal text or none, except cmdline_panel.open below. After each matched hello the add-on also writes one push, devtools.keys: at most 8 rows of a one-character key and an action from a fixed list of four (tree.down, tree.up, tree.collapse, tree.expand), at most 512 bytes. The module turns each action into an untrusted arrow keydown on the focused DevTools element and loads no add-on code into DevTools documents. It sends the module no code, URLs, selectors or page text for the module to run, runs nothing from the hello, and the module sends no raw key events to the add-on, except the characters typed while the command line opens (below) and the keys typed while hint labels show (Hints over Firefox's own UI, below). Hints over Firefox's own UI: the command hint.browser labels the controls of Firefox itself. The state may hold chrome_hint_keys, at most 4 key token lists of at most 4 tokens each, built from the user's keymap, which the module matches with the focus in a dialog, the Library, Page Info or an open panel, never in a field. A whole binding makes the module hold that window's keys and send chrome_hints.want, one argument, a random number. The add-on answers with chrome_hints.collect_here, which names no window. The module takes its own number once, within 3 s and only in the window where the key was typed, so the add-on cannot start a session where the user did not ask. Module to add-on kinds, each checked, at most 4 KB: chrome_hints.targets (control number and box in CSS pixels, at most 400 controls, in at most 32 parts), chrome_hints.key (one typed key of a label alphabet, Backspace, Enter or Tab, with a counter), chrome_hints.end and chrome_hints.want. Add-on to module kinds: chrome_hints.collect (session, window id, label colors as JSON text of hex values, checked by a strict hex test), chrome_hints.draw (control numbers, label letters, typed letters), chrome_hints.pick (session and control number), chrome_hints.clear. The module collects controls itself and runs one fixed action per kind of control on a pick, only for a number it collected in that session. A pick of a control that grants something (a permission Allow, a blocked download, opening a downloaded file, a client certificate, a login, and any control that its table does not name on such a surface) never clicks. It marks the control and waits for the user's own Enter, read from the trusted key event of that window by the module itself, at least 500 ms (security.notification_enable_delay) after the mark, with the same control still showing. No kind confirms. The table of such controls is in the module, since the add-on is the party it guards against. The popup walk (desertfox-popup-walk.js) maps j, k, h and l to arrow keys in open menus and panels, with fixed letters and no kind. Keys on locked pages: the state also holds a pruned prefix tree of the normal keymap (at most 32 KB), whose leaves say only forward or name one of the seven module commands. For a forward leaf the module sends a run request (kind run, at most 512 bytes): the finished match as key tokens and a count, with no tab id. The add-on matches it again against its own stored keymap, refuses a key the keymap does not bind there, a key that needs a page and a count over the command's repeat_limit, and runs the binding through its own router in the active tab. A key that asks for a value sends the module one more request kind, address_bar.open, with the printed command text (at most 4 KB) and the id of the tab that asked, which the module puts in the address bar after df for the user to edit and run, without starting a query, and only while that tab is still selected in the focused window. It is text in an input field, never code or an address to load. The command line itself comes first, through the request kind cmdline_panel.open with one argument, a whole tab id. The module refuses it unless that tab is still selected, then opens a panel holding the add-on's own cmdline.html at a fixed address, in a remote browser built as Firefox builds a toolbar popup: the add-on's process and principal, never the system principal. The page talks to the add-on with runtime messages only. After a key that opens the command line, the module holds that window's keys until the panel or the address bar has the focus (at most 1.5 s) and runs none of them. Its reply to cmdline_panel.open is JSON text of at most 256 bytes: a random key that the module puts in the page's address (cmdline.html?panel=<key>) and the characters typed meanwhile (at most 32). Once the module opened the panel, the add-on records the tab, its window, its private flag, that address and the command text with the typed characters in storage.session. It answers the page's open_panel_cmdline only for a sender with its own extension id, no sender tab and exactly that address, and only once per record, so neither a framed copy, another tab-less copy nor the toolbar popup gets it. When the module refuses or has no panel, the add-on falls back to address_bar.open.
Locked pages: a second setting, browser_module_pages, off by default and a consent setting, lets the module run the add-on's own content.js and bundles in the PDF viewer and Reader View only, in a sandbox with the expanded principal Firefox gives content scripts and never the system principal, with the stand-in for the extension API in locked_shim.js (src/content/locked_shim.ts). The only kinds on the allow list are the ones that code uses: page_call from the page and page_push to it, each answered in its reply's optional value, and page_gone, in which the module says that a page's code ended (a tab id and a counter, no page data). page_call and page_push each carry a message of the add-on's own content script types as JSON text, and the module only relays it, never parsing it to pick an action, address or selector. The add-on refuses a page call from a tab on any other about: page or an extension page. The add-on takes a page call only of a type on a fixed list (LOCKED_PAGE_ROUTES in src/shared/browser_module_protocol.ts), never a type of an extension page, never a snippet, and builds the sender itself from tabs.get of the tab id: frame 0, the tab's own address, no extension id, and from_page set on commands. While both settings are on, the add-on also writes four snapshots to storage.session for that code (the keymap with its site rules, the settings in force, the theme and the which-key list), each with its own size cap of at most 512 KB. Browser code can read that storage. The status bar file (desertfox-statusbar.js) draws a bar in the browser window from that state with createElement and textContent only, checks every field again, applies a theme color only after a strict hex check, reads the tab address, container and scroll place in the browser, and makes no request.

Permissions:
- tabs, webNavigation, sessions, tabGroups, contextualIdentities: tab, window, container and tab group commands, closed-tab undo, and page load state for the stop and media commands.
- bookmarks, history: command line completion and the bookmark commands.
- downloads: the download and save commands. notifications: toasts that report a command result.
- clipboardWrite: copy commands. clipboardRead: the paste commands and registers, read only when the user runs such a command.
- cookies, optional browsingData: the hard reload with cache clear and the site data clear commands.
- storage: settings, keymap and state.
- <all_urls>: the content script runs at document_start in every frame, handles keys and draws hints.
- optional nativeMessaging: the native host above. optional geolocation: the weather card, from its button.

Data collection: required is none. optional is locationInfo, requested with permissions.request from the weather card's button. The card sends only rounded coordinates or the city name the user typed.
